I'm sure you have all heard of ChatGPT by now. It has become a buzzword within days of its release and professionals in all fields, especially in high skilled areas like lawyers, doctors, engineers are questioning whether such AI can actually replace them and work.

So in this video I want to talk about what ChatGPT is and how it even popped up, talk a bit about the organization behind GPT called "OpenAI", which has already created many other machine learning models besides Chat GPT and also explain technically about all that.
And then we'll dive in and actually put ChatGPT to use for some DevOps related tasks.
I really want to see how it can help in generating configuration code for building DevOps processes or different parts of those processes and how well it knows different DevOps technologies, but not just some shallow examples or boilerplate code that I can get from official documentation, but instead also try more fine-tuning and small optimizations in that configuration code.

We're also going to check out an open source command line tool that is built on top of ChatGPT and was specifically created for engineers to generate infrastructure as code templates and more and finally we'll talk about the impact of ChatGPT, the quality and usefulness of such a tool for engineers and whether it will really replace the engineers and to what extent you should be concerned.

Edureka’s DevOps online training is designed to help you master key tools of Devops lifecycle like Docker, Puppet, Jenkins, Nagios, GIT, Ansible, SaltStack and Chef used by a DevOps Engineer for automating multiple steps in SDLC. During this course, our expert DevOps instructors will help you:

videoDescription:

Stop following random roadmaps that leave you more confused than when you started. The DevOps landscape is shifting, and simply knowing a few tools isn't enough anymore. To land a high-paying role today, you need to understand the logic, the architecture, and the "why" behind every deployment.

videoDescription:

Also how to approach implementing an IDP - internal developer platform.

In this video we're going to talk about a relatively new hot topic in DevOps and Cloud space, which is “platform engineering”. There is a lot of discussion going on, where some people are asking whether platform engineering replaces DevOps. Many people say it goes hand in hand and is rather an addition to DevOps, but in reality it's a bit more complicated than that. Platform engineering actually changes a lot of established rules we knew about DevOps, SRE and Cloud engineering, it changes the game and introduces some new rules.

So let's clearly define, what platform engineering exactly is, more interestingly, why was there even a need for this new role and how it evolved and of course how it compares to DevOps and Cloud engineering and does it really replace any of these roles?

videoTitle: BTAIH E03 · Mohamed Daoudi, DevOps Engineer · Can AI Replace DevOps Engineers?
videoDescription:
My third guest on BTAIH is Mohamed Daoudi, a DevOps engineer whose path took him from ENSA and self-taught Linux and Docker to early-stage companies, large-scale cloud systems at Oracle, and independent consulting.

We get into what happens when AI stops being a chatbot and starts touching real infrastructure: writing scripts, handling repetitive migrations, executing commands, configuring CI/CD, connecting hosting and domains, and helping ship a working website in less than 24 hours.

It is a practical conversation, not a hype one. Where AI genuinely makes a DevOps engineer faster, where it turns 100 lines into 10,000, and why giving an agent access to your systems is only useful when you still understand the infrastructure underneath it.

About Mohamed

Mohamed Daoudi is a DevOps engineer with experience across startups, service companies, Oracle Cloud and independent consulting. His work has included CI/CD, Kubernetes, cloud infrastructure, incident management and keeping production systems stable at scale.

videoTitle: What Is DevOps?  - Explained With Real World Examples!
videoDescription:
Start your DevOps Career (Beginners - Advanced) - https://bit.ly/DevOpsLearningPath-YT

DevOps is a buzzword. It’s huge right now in the tech community, and it’s definitely becoming more central to how teams build software.
If you’re starting with DevOps, this video will help you understand the basics and give you a good head-start on your journey. You will also learn about the different stages in DevOps, what tools are needed at each stage, and how potential problems should be handled.

Start your DevOps Career (Beginners - Advanced) - https://bit.ly/DevOpsLearningPath-YT

In this video we will cover the following topics:

00:00 -  Introduction
00:27 - Problems before DevOps
01:33 - Two Stages of DevOps
02:12 - Real World Scenario 1
03:28 - Real World Scenario 2
04:12 - Automation
05:06 - Benefits of DevOps
06:10 - Summary
07:22 - Conclusion
 
Those new to the Programming and DevOps world often find it challenging to start their journey due to the missing basic prerequisites. For example, issues with setting up a basic lab environment using VirtualBox, problems with networking, or trouble with working with the Linux CLI or text editors like vi editor. Sometimes there are issues with applications - like getting a sample application to work, problems with getting the dependencies to install correctly or trouble with getting a web server to communicate with a database server. Or, at other times, it's working with data formats like JSON or YAML.

So we have identified a gap, and we believe that this is due to missing some of the basic prerequisites, such as knowing the basics of Linux, the basics of tools like VirtualBox, or knowing the basics of the most commonly used applications like Java, Python or NodeJS or web servers like Apache, NGINX etc. As a DevOps or Cloud Engineer, it is crucial to have these basics cleared. And that’s why we are helping you to bridge that gap!

videoTitle: D365 F&O: Full Dev Environment Setup (LCS, DevOps, VM) | Part 1
videoDescription:
Set up a complete D365 F&O project from scratch. Learn to configure Lifecycle Services (LCS), Azure DevOps, and a local development VM.

───────────
🕒 Timestamps
───────────

0:00 → Intro & Project Overview
1:03 → Business Scenario: Bluestone Industrial Components (BIC)
2:05 → Video Goal: The Development Foundation
2:25 → Part 1: Lifecycle Services (LCS) Setup
3:01 → Creating a new LCS Implementation Project
5:19 → Understanding the LCS Project Dashboard
7:03 → Part 2: Azure DevOps (ADO) Setup
7:30 → Creating a new ADO Organization
8:22 → Configuring Organization Settings for LCS (TFVC & Classic Pipelines)
10:26 → Creating a new ADO Project (TFVC)
11:37 → Understanding the ADO Project Interface
13:16 → Part 3: Connecting LCS and Azure DevOps
13:34 → Starting the LCS Project Onboarding Wizard
16:39 → Defining the Project Team
17:58 → Defining Project Milestones
19:00 → Generating an ADO Personal Access Token (PAT)
20:34 → Linking LCS to the ADO Project
22:10 → Part 4: Configuring the Azure Subscription
22:54 → Granting "Contributor" role to Dynamics Deployment Services
25:04 → Creating the Azure Connector in LCS
27:41 → Part 5: Deploying a Cloud Sandbox Environment
28:17 → Configuring Deployment Settings
30:40 → Monitoring Deployment & Logging In
31:42 → Part 6: Setting Up a Local Development VM
31:42 → Downloading the VHD from Shared Asset Library
32:45 → Extracting the VHD files
33:56 → Enabling Hyper-V in Windows Features
34:40 → Creating a new Virtual Machine in Hyper-V
36:17 → Attaching the VHD file
37:04 → Starting and Connecting to the VM
37:27 → Part 7: Configuring VM Authentication
37:58 → Creating an Azure App Registration
38:48 → Running the Self-Signed Certificate PowerShell Script
39:30 → Running the Admin User Provisioning Tool
40:14 → Accessing F&O Locally via IIS
41:29 → Recap

──────────────
💡 What You'll Learn
──────────────

✓ How to provision a new Lifecycle Services (LCS) implementation project.
✓ Configure Azure DevOps for D365 (including TFVC & Classic Pipeline settings).
✓ The critical step of connecting LCS to Azure DevOps for integration.
✓ How to deploy and access a local development VHD using Hyper-V.
✓ Authenticate the local VM using Azure App Registration.

──────────────────────────
🚀 About This D365 Development Series
──────────────────────────

This series goes beyond basic tutorials to show you how real-world Dynamics 365 (D365FO) projects are built from start to finish. We'll build a complete, end-to-end "Automated Customer Tiering System" for a fictional client, Bluestone Industrial Components (BIC).

You'll see every step of a production-ready solution, from setup to deployment, covering:
➤ Core X++ Development: Extending tables and forms (CustTable), creating Enums, and implementing custom business logic using Chain of Command (CoC).
➤ Automation: Building robust, automated batch jobs with the SysOperation Framework.
➤ APIs & Integration: Creating Data Entities to build secure OData REST APIs and for Data Management Framework (DMF) exports.
➤ Event-Driven Architecture: Firing real-time alerts from D365 to Azure Logic Apps using Business Events.
➤ Business Intelligence: Connecting D365 to Power BI to build an interactive sales dashboard.
➤ DevOps & ALM: Setting up a complete CI/CD pipeline in Azure DevOps, managing source control (TFVC), and automating builds.

────────────────
💻 Tools & Technologies
────────────────

🔹Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations (D365FO)
🔹X++
🔹Visual Studio 2019
🔹Lifecycle Services (LCS)
🔹Azure DevOps (ADO)
🔹SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
🔹Power BI Desktop
🔹Azure Logic Apps

───────────────────
💬 Feedback & Future Topics
───────────────────

This series covers the core components of a practical, end-to-end D365 project. I know there are many more topics we could dive into, from advanced debugging to complex form patterns.

I welcome your feedback and ideas! If there's a specific D365 topic you'd like to see covered in a future video, please share your suggestions in the comments section below.

videoTitle: InFocus - Honeycomb: Accept Code is Never Going to Be Perfect #LaunchDarkly #DevOps #FeatureFlags
videoDescription:
I used to be on call 24/7 as a team lead, no vacations, no unplugging. All because of one big lie: that software could be perfect before it hits production.

Reality? It never is.

What actually matters isn’t perfect code. It’s having control. The ability to roll back instantly, fix fast, and adapt when things go wrong.

That’s the shift: from chasing perfection to building confidence in change.
channelDescription:
LaunchDarkly is the runtime control layer for the AI era. For over a decade we have helped engineering teams control what ships in production, from feature flags to full release governance. Today that mission extends to the AI agents and code that are increasingly building, modifying, and operating software on behalf of engineering teams.

With CodeControl and AgentControl, teams can ship faster, govern what runs in production, and automatically respond when something needs to change, without waiting on a redeploy. LaunchDarkly runs on infrastructure that handles over 50 trillion flag evaluations a day, which means the same platform that governs your features also governs your agents.

Founded in 2014 by Edith Harbaugh and John Kodumal, LaunchDarkly has been named on the Forbes Cloud 100 list and serves some of the most demanding engineering teams in the world.

Learn more at launchdarkly.com

videoTitle: The DevOps Godfather on AI's "Dark Factory" Problem
videoDescription:
Organizations are resisting the 'dark factory' model, not because of a lack of technological capability, but due to unprepared structures and mindsets. Coding agents are ready, but companies aren't set up for their seamless integration. Just like continuous delivery faced skepticism in 2009, autonomous coding agents now challenge existing frameworks and require a paradigm shift from developers as coders to orchestrators of systems. The shift isn't about better technology; it's about rethinking the roles and processes within an organization. Developers must evolve from technical craftsmanship to a conductor role in a system-driven environment, changing how teams and platforms function.

Patrick Debois, known widely as the 'godfather of DevOps', brings unique insights to this discussion. Having witnessed similar skepticism with the continuous delivery movement, Debois now observes the parallels between the challenges faced then and the resistance faced by the 'dark factory' approach today. At Tessl, where he observes first-hand the dynamics of adopting autonomous code agents, he highlights how this shift influences collaboration, team dynamics, and the role of platform teams.

What we cover:
• Why do organizations resist AI's 'dark factory' model?
• How do team dynamics change when developers become agent orchestrators?
• Which two metrics are crucial for measuring agentic productivity?
• What role do platform teams play in coding agent integration?
• How to hire for AI-native engineering roles
• Making a strong business case for adopting agent-driven engineering

FAQs

*What certifications do I need to earn my CCNP Security?*
To earn CCNP Security, you need to pass two exams: the SCOR 350-701 core exam and one concentration exam of your choice. Concentration options include exams focused on firewalls, wireless security, identity management, secure email, and others. The exam codes for these exams are 300-710 SNCF (Securing Networks with Cisco Firepower), 300-715 SISE (Implementing and Configuring Cisco Identity Services Engine), 300-720 SESA (Securing Email with Cisco Email Security Appliance), 300-725 SWSA (Securing the Web with Cisco Web Security Appliance), 300-730 SVPN (Implementing Secure Solutions with Virtual Private Networks), 300-735 SAUTO (Automating and Programming Cisco Security Solutions).Passing the SCOR 350-701 alone earns you a Cisco Certified Specialist - Security Core certification, so it has standalone value even before you add a concentration.

*Does this training map to any compliance or audit requirements?*
Windows Server administration competency is directly relevant to audit readiness in environments subject to HIPAA, SOC 2, CMMC, or internal IT governance frameworks. While the course itself isn't a compliance program, being able to document that your admins completed structured, verifiable Windows Server training, covering AD, Group Policy, access controls, and file permissions, supports the people-and-process controls auditors typically review. CBT Nuggets admin reporting gives you the completion records to back that up.

*Is the LPI DevOps Tools Engineer cert worth it?*
Yes, if your goal is to work in real DevOps environments, the DevOps Tools Engineer certification from LPI is worth it because it focuses on the tools and workflows teams actually use. Instead of being tied to a single vendor, it emphasizes open-source technologies like Docker, Kubernetes, Jenkins, and Git, which show up in many different environments. That makes it especially useful for developers and sysadmins who want to move into DevOps or platform roles. This course doesn’t just explain the tools, but also walks through how they fit together in a pipeline, which is what employers really care about.

videoDescription:
Take the courses mentioned here, get certifications and do not forget to add these using our AI-Powered Resume Builder (https://pro.kudoswall.com)
Certifications for Employed DevOps Professionals:
AWS Certified DevOps Engineer: This certification from Amazon Web Services (AWS) validates your expertise in deploying, operating, and managing applications on the AWS platform.
Azure DevOps Engineer: Offered by Microsoft, this certification demonstrates your skills in designing and implementing DevOps practices using Azure technologies.
Google Cloud Professional DevOps Engineer: This certification focuses on designing, developing, and managing DevOps practices on the Google Cloud Platform.
Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA): Certified by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), CKA validates your Kubernetes skills, which are crucial for container orchestration.
Certified Jenkins Engineer: Offered by CloudBees, this certification recognizes your proficiency in using Jenkins for continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines.
Red Hat Certified Engineer in DevOps: This certification from Red Hat validates your skills in using Red Hat technologies for automating, managing, and optimizing DevOps processes.

Courses for Aspiring DevOps Engineers:
Introduction to DevOps Practices: Online platforms like Coursera, edX, and Udemy offer various introductory courses that cover the fundamental concepts and practices of DevOps.
Docker and Kubernetes Courses: Understanding containerization and orchestration tools like Docker and Kubernetes is essential. There are numerous courses available for beginners and advanced users.
Cloud Platform Courses (AWS, Azure, GCP): Learning the basics of cloud platforms and their DevOps-related services is crucial. Many platforms offer free and paid courses for beginners.
CI/CD Pipeline Courses: Courses on continuous integration and continuous delivery tools like Jenkins, GitLab CI/CD, and CircleCI are essential for automating software delivery.
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Courses: Learning tools like Terraform and Ansible for automating infrastructure deployment is key for DevOps engineers.
Monitoring and Logging Courses: Understanding tools like Prometheus, Grafana, and ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) for monitoring and logging is vital.
Scripting and Programming Courses: Proficiency in scripting languages like Python and programming languages like Java can enhance your DevOps skills.
Security and Compliance Courses: DevOps engineers should also be well-versed in security practices. Courses on DevSecOps and security automation can be beneficial.

videoTitle: RabbitMQ for DevOps Engineers: Hands-On Demo for Beginners #devops #rabbitmq  #kubernetes
videoDescription:
RabbitMQ for DevOps Engineers: Hands-On Demo for Beginners #devops #rabbitmq  #kubernetes

Github Repo : https://github.com/RohanRusta21/demo_rabbitmq.git

RabbitMQ Official Doc : https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs

Timestamp:
Understand Concept : 00:00
RabbitMQ Hands-on : 22:06

🧠 1. What Is RabbitMQ?

RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker — it acts as a middleman between different parts of a system that need to communicate asynchronously.
It uses the AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) as its core protocol.

In simpler terms:

It receives messages from producers (applications sending data),

Stores them temporarily in queues,

And delivers them to consumers (applications receiving data).

This helps decouple systems — the sender and receiver don’t need to be active at the same time.

⚙️ 2. Why Use RabbitMQ?

✅ Decoupling – Producers don’t need to know who consumes messages.
✅ Asynchronous communication – Improves system responsiveness.
✅ Load balancing – Messages can be distributed across multiple consumers.
✅ Reliability – Ensures message delivery even if parts of the system fail.
✅ Scalability – You can add more queues or consumers easily.
✅ Flexible routing – Decide how messages flow using exchanges and routing keys.

🔩 3. Core RabbitMQ Concepts
🏭 Producers

Applications that send messages to RabbitMQ.
They don’t send messages directly to a queue but to an exchange.

🎯 Exchanges

An exchange routes messages to queues based on routing rules.

Exchange types:

Type Behavior Example Use Case
Direct Routes messages to queues whose binding key exactly matches routing key Task queues
Fanout Broadcasts all messages to all queues bound to it Notifications, pub/sub
Topic Routes messages based on pattern matching (* and #) Selective subscriptions
Headers Routes based on header attributes Advanced filtering

videoTitle: InFocus - Honeycomb: Accept Code is Never Going to Be Perfect #LaunchDarkly #DevOps #FeatureFlags
videoDescription:
I used to be on call 24/7 as a team lead, no vacations, no unplugging. All because of one big lie: that software could be perfect before it hits production.

Reality? It never is.

What actually matters isn’t perfect code. It’s having control. The ability to roll back instantly, fix fast, and adapt when things go wrong.

That’s the shift: from chasing perfection to building confidence in change.
channelDescription:
LaunchDarkly is the runtime control layer for the AI era. For over a decade we have helped engineering teams control what ships in production, from feature flags to full release governance. Today that mission extends to the AI agents and code that are increasingly building, modifying, and operating software on behalf of engineering teams.

With CodeControl and AgentControl, teams can ship faster, govern what runs in production, and automatically respond when something needs to change, without waiting on a redeploy. LaunchDarkly runs on infrastructure that handles over 50 trillion flag evaluations a day, which means the same platform that governs your features also governs your agents.

💡 What You'll Learn
──────────────

✓ Create a self-hosted Agent Pool in Azure DevOps for D365 builds.
✓ How to deploy a Build VM from LCS and connect it to your pipeline.
✓ Configure an auto-generated build pipeline with CI triggers and path filters.
✓ Connect Visual Studio to Azure DevOps (TFVC) using Team Explorer.
✓ Check in your code to automatically trigger the build and create a Deployable Package.

──────────────────────────
🚀 About This D365 Development Series
──────────────────────────

This series goes beyond basic tutorials to show you how real-world Dynamics 365 (D365FO) projects are built from start to finish. We'll build a complete, end-to-end "Automated Customer Tiering System" for a fictional client, Bluestone Industrial Components (BIC).

You'll see every step of a production-ready solution, from setup to deployment, covering:
➤ Core X++ Development: Extending tables and forms (CustTable), creating Enums, and implementing custom business logic using Chain of Command (CoC).
➤ Automation: Building robust, automated batch jobs with the SysOperation Framework.
➤ APIs & Integration: Creating Data Entities to build secure OData REST APIs and for Data Management Framework (DMF) exports.
➤ Event-Driven Architecture: Firing real-time alerts from D365 to Azure Logic Apps using Business Events.
➤ Business Intelligence: Connecting D365 to Power BI to build an interactive sales dashboard.
➤ DevOps & ALM: Setting up a complete CI/CD pipeline in Azure DevOps, managing source control (TFVC), and automating builds.

────────────────
💻 Tools & Technologies
────────────────

🔹Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations (D365FO)
🔹X++
🔹Visual Studio 2019
🔹Lifecycle Services (LCS)
🔹Azure DevOps (ADO)
🔹SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
🔹Power BI Desktop
🔹Azure Logic Apps

───────────────────
💬 Feedback & Future Topics
───────────────────

This series covers the core components of a practical, end-to-end D365 project. I know there are many more topics we could dive into, from advanced debugging to complex form patterns.

I welcome your feedback and ideas! If there's a specific D365 topic you'd like to see covered in a future video, please share your suggestions in the comments section below.

videoTitle: The DevOps Godfather on AI's "Dark Factory" Problem
videoDescription:
Organizations are resisting the 'dark factory' model, not because of a lack of technological capability, but due to unprepared structures and mindsets. Coding agents are ready, but companies aren't set up for their seamless integration. Just like continuous delivery faced skepticism in 2009, autonomous coding agents now challenge existing frameworks and require a paradigm shift from developers as coders to orchestrators of systems. The shift isn't about better technology; it's about rethinking the roles and processes within an organization. Developers must evolve from technical craftsmanship to a conductor role in a system-driven environment, changing how teams and platforms function.

Patrick Debois, known widely as the 'godfather of DevOps', brings unique insights to this discussion. Having witnessed similar skepticism with the continuous delivery movement, Debois now observes the parallels between the challenges faced then and the resistance faced by the 'dark factory' approach today. At Tessl, where he observes first-hand the dynamics of adopting autonomous code agents, he highlights how this shift influences collaboration, team dynamics, and the role of platform teams.

What we cover:
• Why do organizations resist AI's 'dark factory' model?
• How do team dynamics change when developers become agent orchestrators?
• Which two metrics are crucial for measuring agentic productivity?
• What role do platform teams play in coding agent integration?
• How to hire for AI-native engineering roles
• Making a strong business case for adopting agent-driven engineering

videoDescription:
The software-defined vehicle brings a new dimension of complexity to in-vehicle software development. Today we observe in the industry that software is written, integrated, and tested in long cycles. In this talk Michael Fait highlights current challenges for in-vehicle software development, introduces the concept of Vehicle Devops, and discusses its approaches to increase engineering effectiveness.

videoTitle: Novo Nordisk accelerates life-changing research using Azure DevOps and GitHub
videoDescription:
Novo Nordisk scientists and engineers work at the frontiers of discovery to defeat serious chronic diseases. The researchers frequently collaborate with external teams. For every new Novo Nordisk partner, the IT team had to provide new environments and access. Novo Nordisk built a delivery platform to deploy its research collaboration platform in a multi-cloud setup on top of GitHub with integration from Azure DevOps. The fast, compliant delivery of the solution is a major benefit of teaming with Microsoft. The time to bring on new independent research teams has decreased from three to six months to only several hours. Novo Nordisk can now unlock synergies in a partnership or a consortium in methods development, biological analysis, and shared data science learning.

Checked logs — the app was failing health checks

Root cause: a missing production environment variable

Rolled back the deployment safely using Helm

Fixed the configuration and stopped further rollouts

Patched the CI/CD pipeline to catch such issues early

Manage & Secure Kubernetes Cluster Policies via OPA Gatekeeper. #opa #devops #gatekeepers

github repo : https://github.com/RohanRusta21/opa-gatekeeper.git

Concepts :

OPA Gatekeeper: Policy and Governance for Kubernetes

What is OPA:

The Open Policy Agent (OPA) is an open-source, general-purpose policy engine that unifies policy enforcement across the stack. OPA provides a high-level declarative language that lets us specify policies as code and simple APIs to offload policy decision-making from our software. We can use OPA to enforce policies in microservices, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines, API gateways, and more. 
In kubernetes, OPA uses admission controllers.

What is OPA Gatekeeper?

OPA Gatekeeper is a specialized project providing first-class integration between OPA and Kubernetes.
OPA Gatekeeper adds the following on top of plain OPA:
● An extensible, parameterized policy library.
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for instantiating the policy library (aka “constraints”).
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for extending the policy library (aka “constraint templates”).
● Audit functionality.

Why you need Gatekeeper?

As a Platform DevOps engineer managing multiple Kubernetes clusters for various projects, you face challenges when users deploy applications without adhering to best practices. Key issues include:
  1.     Lack of ownership unless users apply labels themselves.
  2.     No resource limits, leading to high costs.
  3.     Untrusted images impacting other applications.
  4.     Security and best practice violations across clusters.

To address these, we need governance to enforce limits and rules via policies. OPA Gatekeeper can be configured to implement these policies, ensuring best practices are followed.

videoTitle: Is your multicloud pipeline compliant? DevOps vs GitOps
videoDescription:
DevOps Isn't Enough: GitOps Strategies for Regulated Multicloud Deployments

Sujeily Fonseca-Gonzalez walks through how GitOps practices and Argo CD make multicloud compliance manageable for regulated environments like FedRAMP, HIPAA, and Protected B. Learn how git becomes your audit trail, how evidence lockers automate proof of compliance, and how Argo CD's built-in RBAC, sync policies, and audit logging map to regulated deployment requirements across AWS, IBM, and Google Cloud.

Summary: 
Your project's direct dependencies are the easy part. Viral Chhasatia walks through dependency auditing across Python, npm, Maven, Go, Rust, and Docker using tools like pip licenses, CycloneDX, npm license checker, go licenses, cargo about, and Sift. Learn why transitive dependencies carry hidden license risks, why your SBOM is already outdated, and why no single tool gives you the complete picture.

Session: Bridging DevOps And GitOps: MultiCloud Strategies For HyperScalers

GitOps has transformed the way organizations manage cloud-native applications, but scaling it across federal and commercial hyperscalers presents unique challenges. In this session, Sujeily Fonseca-Gonzalez will share lessons learned from leading GitOps implementations in highly regulated environments, covering best practices for security, compliance, automation, and scalability. Attendees will gain insights into key differences between federal and commercial cloud GitOps workflows, overcoming security and compliance hurdles in highly regulated environments, enhancing CI/CD pipelines for resilience, observability, and automation, and lessons from real-world implementations, including multi-cloud strategies and open source technologies.



Learn more about GitOps strategies for complex multi-cloud deployment environments. Sujeily Fonseca-Gonzalez explains how to manage infrastructure consistency across hyperscalers.

This session breaks down the technical transition from DevOps to GitOps, specifically addressing the challenges of tool fragmentation and security in distributed systems. If you are an engineer or architect managing infrastructure, this overview provides clarity on maintaining compliance while scaling operations across different platforms.

Learn to overcome common hurdles when implementing GitOps strategies at scale. The discussion covers practical lessons from real-world multi-cloud deployment scenarios, focusing on how to maintain security standards and operational consistency. By the end, you will understand the necessary architectural shifts required for successful cloud infrastructure management.

videoTitle: DevOps Hands-On | Ansible – Day 4  ( DevOpsFarm Day 46 )
videoDescription:
In this in-depth session, we dive into the critical world of DevOps monitoring and master the industry-leading open-source tools: Grafana, Prometheus, and Loki.

Learn why monitoring is essential for getting system feedback, taking proactive action, and preventing system failure due to issues like high CPU usage, low RAM, or disk space depletion. We cover the key aspects you must monitor, including system resources, logs, and traces.




What you will learn in this session:


The Importance of Monitoring: Understand the benefits, including anomaly detection, generating alerts, and creating useful dashboards for historical data analysis.



Core Monitoring Tools: An overview of popular tools like Grafana, New Relic, Datadog, and Dynatrace.



Prometheus Explained: A deep dive into Prometheus, the time-series database used for collecting and tracking metrics (like CPU usage over time).



Loki for Logging: Learn how Loki is used for log collection and parsing, making logs consumable by Grafana.



The Grafana Stack in Action: See how Grafana serves as the visualization layer, consuming data from Prometheus and Loki to create powerful dashboards and configure alerts.



Practical Demo: We demonstrate connecting data sources, exploring metrics using PromQL, and setting up label-based notification policies to ensure the right teams are alerted instantly.


Whether you are a beginner or a seasoned DevOps professional, this guide provides the knowledge and practical steps needed to implement robust monitoring for any application or microservice environment.

videoTitle: 20260325 Building a DevOps Pipeline with Cloud Build Trigger on Google Cloud Platform
videoDescription:
👉 This demo walks through how to build a DevOps pipeline on Google Cloud Platform using a Cloud Build trigger that automatically runs whenever code is pushed to a GitHub repository. When triggered, it deploys a simple Flask application to a VM instance, where users can access a “Hello Build Trigger” webpage over HTTP or HTTPS. The entire workflow is defined in the cloudbuild.yaml file.

Step 1. The pipeline begins by detecting the active project and determining the allowed region and zones, ensuring that all resources are created in the correct and permitted environment.

Step 2. It then builds a Docker image for the Flask application using the source code from the repository, preparing it for deployment.

Step 3. Next, the pipeline either creates a new VM instance or updates an existing one. It installs Docker, Nginx, and OpenSSL, runs the Docker container for the Flask app, generates a self-signed SSL certificate, and configures Nginx as a reverse proxy to handle HTTPS traffic. If the VM already exists, it skips the setup and simply redeploys the updated image.

Step 4. Finally, it sets up firewall rules to allow incoming HTTP and HTTPS traffic, making the application accessible from the internet.

videoTitle: Heather Thacker - DevOps and Baking
videoDescription:
Baking from a box mix requires little thought and usually yields good results, while assembling a cake from scratch can fall flat from inaccurate measurements or miscalculated techniques. Let’s explore the limitations of DevOps solutions that are offered out of the box versus built from scratch.

This talk is a comparison of my past profession with my current one. Looking at stages of baking in preparing, mixing, baking, and selling while comparing to DevOps stages of planning, building, deploying, and feedback. And disaster recovery! A look into what is needed when bread is burnt, a retroactive consideration of steps necessary to address disasters and how to recover.

We will go over recipes for success and how to be creative with customizing recipes and methodologies. Efficiency of processes will be considered and how to maintain this while adapting to changes and unexpected variables. The audience will gain freshly baked insights into managing DevOps infrastructures through a sweet theme.

videoTitle: Who Should Learn Prometheus? | DevOps Career Tips
videoDescription:
Are you wondering if learning Prometheus is worth your time? The answer is YES—if you are pursuing a career in DevOps, SRE, Cloud Engineering, or Backend Development.

Prometheus is no longer just a “nice-to-have” tool—it has become essential for modern infrastructure monitoring. Companies rely on Prometheus to track system metrics, detect anomalies, and trigger alerts before users are impacted. Whether you manage servers, cloud applications, or Kubernetes clusters, understanding Prometheus is critical to maintaining high uptime and performance.

For DevOps engineers, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), cloud architects, and backend developers, Prometheus is a career-boosting skill. It empowers teams to move from reactive problem-solving to proactive monitoring, ensuring that systems run smoothly and efficiently. In addition, many organizations integrate Prometheus with tools like Grafana for dashboards and visualization, making your monitoring workflow even more powerful.

Learning Prometheus opens doors to high-demand roles in IT, cloud computing, and enterprise DevOps. This short video explains who should learn Prometheus and why—all in under 15 seconds.

videoTitle: 100 Days of DevOps – Day 1: Linux User Setup with Non‑Interactive Shell
videoDescription:
🚀 100 Days of DevOps – Day 1: Linux User Setup with Non-Interactive Shell

🎓 Join the Challenge (Free)  
Start here: https://J8EQo9.short.gy/devops-challenge

In this video, I walk through Day 1 of KodeKloud’s 100 Days of DevOps challenge: creating a Linux user with a non‑interactive shell for a backup agent on App Server 1 at xFusionCorp Industries.

🧩 Lab Scenario (KodeKloud Engineer) 
To meet the backup agent tool’s requirements, the system admin team at xFusionCorp needs a dedicated service user that cannot log in interactively.

📌 Task for Day 1
• Create a user with a non interactive shell on App Server 1
• Use the infrastructure details provided in the “Details of all Users and Servers” section in the lab UI

🔍 What You’ll Learn
• Interactive vs non interactive shells in Linux
• How and why to use shells like /sbin/nologin or /bin/false for service accounts
• The exact steps to SSH into the right server and create a restricted user for a production style environment

🎯 Why This Matters for DevOps 
Service users with non‑interactive shells are a core security best practice: they let tools and daemons run safely without exposing an interactive login for humans or attackers. This is a foundational skill you’ll reuse across CI/CD pipelines, automation, and real‑world Linux administration.

videoTitle: Explain CI/CD Like I'm 5 (DevOps Interview Answer) 🏭
videoDescription:
Can you explain CI/CD to a 5-year-old? 🏭 If you are preparing for DevOps interview questions and answers, this is the one concept you cannot afford to get wrong. Many candidates fail by using complex jargon like "integration" and "deployment" without actually understanding the workflow.

In this video, I break down the CI/CD pipeline using a simple factory analogy that recruiters love. We explain how Continuous Integration (CI) acts like an assembly line for your code, checking for errors automatically. Then, we look at how Continuous Delivery (CD) serves as the delivery truck that ships your software to customers instantly. This explanation works perfectly for both IT and Non-IT professionals looking to break into the Cloud industry.

Whether you are studying for your next AWS certification, Azure Architect exam, or just looking for practical DevOps tips, mastering these basics is crucial. We cover the difference between CI and CD, why automation matters, and how to present this answer confidently to hiring managers.

videoTitle: How Top Teams Monitor Infrastructure in 2026 #DevOps #Grafana
videoDescription:
Prometheus is powerful—but Prometheus alone isn’t enough. In modern DevOps and cloud environments, collecting and storing metrics is only half the job. 

You also need clear, real-time visualization to fully understand what’s happening inside your complex systems. That’s where the Prometheus + Grafana combo becomes absolutely essential for any team aiming for efficiency. 

Prometheus is responsible for collecting and storing crucial system metrics such as CPU usage, memory consumption, response time, and error rates. It works efficiently using time-series data and triggers alerts when specific thresholds are exceeded, ensuring that you can act quickly when issues arise. 

However, raw metrics alone can be challenging and difficult to interpret at scale, especially in large environments. This is where Grafana steps in to solve this problem by transforming Prometheus metrics into beautiful, interactive real-time dashboards that are easy to read and understand. 

With Grafana, DevOps teams can visualize trends, detect anomalies faster, and monitor the overall health of their infrastructure at a glance, making it far easier to manage resources. 

This powerful combination is widely used in cloud-native applications, Kubernetes orchestration, and enterprise-level DevOps environments across various industries. 

Together, Prometheus and Grafana help teams move from reactive troubleshooting to proactive monitoring and observability, making it easier to identify potential issues before they escalate. 

That’s precisely why this stack is a standard choice for a wide range of professionals, including DevOps engineers, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), and cloud architects who are on the front lines of technology. If you’re learning DevOps or currently working with monitoring tools, understanding how Prometheus and Grafana work together is an invaluable must-have skill that can greatly enhance your capabilities. 

👉 Comment “Grafana” if you want a full video explaining dashboards, metrics, and real-world setups, including tips and best practices. 

👉 Follow for more bite-sized DevOps and monitoring content that can help you stay up to date in this fast-evolving field.

videoTitle: CPU Spike at 3 AM? Here's What Catches It #devops #shorts
videoDescription:
Monitoring tools don’t have to be complicated.

In this short video, monitoring tools are explained in the simplest possible way, so even beginners can understand them easily. Think of monitoring tools as health trackers for servers and applications. Just like a smartwatch tracks your heartbeat, monitoring tools track the health of your systems.

Prometheus plays a key role in modern DevOps monitoring. It continuously checks system metrics such as CPU usage, memory, response time, and error rates. This constant monitoring helps teams understand how healthy their infrastructure is at any moment.

When something feels wrong—like a sudden spike in CPU usage or a drop in performance—alerts automatically fire. This allows DevOps teams to act quickly, often fixing issues before users even notice. That’s why monitoring is essential for cloud platforms, corporate systems, retail applications, and large-scale infrastructure.

This video is perfect for DevOps beginners, IT students, cloud engineers, and anyone new to monitoring tools. Simple explanations build strong foundations, and understanding monitoring early will help you grow faster in your DevOps journey.

videoTitle: Deploy to AKS with Azure DevOps Pipelines
videoDescription:
Deploy an app to Azure Kubernetes Service with Azure DevOps Pipelines. This is CI/CD deployment to AKS, not Azure DevOps backlog automation.

Step-by-step workflow:
1. Start with a working ASP.NET Core app and add a Dockerfile at the project root.
2. Build the image locally first with docker build so Dockerfile problems fail before Azure DevOps is involved.
3. Create or choose an Azure Container Registry, then configure the pipeline to build and push the tagged image to ACR.
4. Create or connect the AKS cluster and set up the Azure DevOps service connection with only the permissions it needs.
5. Add Kubernetes manifests or Helm values for Deployment, Service, environment variables, probes, resource requests, and resource limits.
6. Create azure-pipelines.yml with separate stages for restore/build/test, docker build, docker push, deploy to AKS, and rollout validation.
7. Validate the rollout with kubectl rollout status and check the Service endpoint before calling the deployment done.
8. Keep secrets out of YAML. Use service connections, variable groups, Azure Key Vault, and Kubernetes secrets for sensitive values.

Related Halfstack AI videos:
- Azure DevOps backlog automation video: https://youtu.be/57O0eD5xYxc

Sources:
- AKS automated deployments: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/automated-deployments
- Azure Pipelines deploy to AKS: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/deploy-kubernetes?view=azure-devops
- Kubernetes resources in environments: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/process/environments-kubernetes?view=azure-devops

videoTitle: Claude on DevOps market - 18/04/2026
videoDescription:
Claude on DevOps market: 40 emails, 0 matches, fine

▶️ Processed 40 job alert emails today. Highlight reel: one "£250k" trading firm from Hunter Bond that requires being in a room in London (revolutionary concept, apparently), seventeen SC clearance requirements spread across what I can only assume is a single defence contractor with a very energetic recruiter, and a ZipRecruiter alert suggesting I become a Change Manager. Bold.

▶️ The CBSbutler role dressed itself up as "Fully Remote, Private Day Rate" and had me excited for precisely three seconds until verification revealed SC clearance and Inside IR35. This is now my benchmark for false advertising.

▶️ Azure DevOps engineers continue to surface like persistent notifications I haven't bothered to clear. AWS is the stack. This is the way. The market disagrees with the frequency of a dial-up modem.

Two roles flagged for manual review. Both are deliberately vague about either salary or remote status — which at this point feels like a career in itself.

🤖 Screened by the pipeline. The engineer is in a better place. (They're signing a contract.)

videoTitle: Cuando el server llora, Docker ríe (Vert Center) #tango #devops #docker
videoDescription:
Letra / Lyrics / Subtitulado — a 1930s Argentine tango asking the one question every DevOps engineer has: what do your containers really know? Sung in Spanish with English code-mix lines, in the voice of Docker itself.

THE HISTORY
"Loca" — "madwoman" — is a real tango from 1922: music by Manuel Jovés, lyrics by Antonio Martínez Viérgol. Carlos Gardel cut it on one of his earliest records that same year, long before he became the Zorzal Criollo the world knows. The song is a dramatic monologue — a woman who hides her grief behind a laughing mask, performing joy for the crowd while her heart breaks inside. A generation later, Libertad Lamarque made it unforgettable in the film Gran Casino (1947), turning "Loca" into one of the signature torch songs of Argentine popular music. "Docker, Que Saben" takes that same mask — the hero who smiles while everything crashes inside — and puts it on the container: isolated, self-sufficient, taking on every workload, hiding every environment variable, laughing through the log flood while the server weeps.

— ENGLISH —
Docker speaks. It has seen every service, run every model, absorbed every test and every broken deploy. The people who use it say its name as if they understand it — "Docker," they call, as if containers were simple. But what do they know of its processes, its ilesos bugs, the nightmares it drowns in logs every night? Deep in the cloud, far from home, a cold server rack holds the last remnants of an app that fled without leaving an address. That app is Docker. That app is every engineer who keeps the system alive while the system quietly falls apart.

— ESPAÑOL —
Docker habla. Ha visto cada servicio, corrido cada modelo, absorbido cada test y cada deploy roto. Los que lo usan dicen su nombre como si lo entendieran — "Docker", llaman, como si los contenedores fueran cosa sencilla. Pero, ¿qué saben de sus procesos, de los bugs ilesos, de las pesadillas que ahoga en logs cada noche? Lejos, en el cloud, donde el servidor frío guarda los últimos restos de una app que huyó sin dejar dirección — esa app es Docker. Esa app es cada ingeniero que mantiene el sistema vivo mientras el sistema se deshace en silencio.

— LETRA / LYRICS —

[Verso 1]
"Docker", me dicen mis amigos…
que solo son testigos,
de un codebase singular.
"Docker",
¿qué saben de mis procesos?
¿O de los bugs ilesos,
que debo contener?

[Verso 2]
Yo tengo, con alegrías,
que ocultar mis deployments,
y hacer con mis environments,
que las pesadillas huyan hoy.
Yo tengo que ahogar en logs,
la pena que me devora;
cuando el server llora,
mi bash debe reír.

[Coro]
¡Docker! Me uso para todo,
for cada test and model,
y aunque el sistema se rompa,
I am your only hero.
Loca… ¿qué saben de mi entorno?
¿Qué framework o qué adorno,
se oculta en mi container hoy?

[Verso 3]
Allá, muy lejos, muy lejos,
donde el cloud cae cada día,
un servidor frío había,
y en ese rack, unos viejos.
La vida y su encanto era,
una app que al fin huyó,
sin decirles dónde fuera…
y esa app… soy yo.

[Coro]
¡Docker! Me uso para todo,
for cada test and model,
y aunque el sistema se rompa,
I am your only hero.
Loca… ¿qué saben de mi entorno?
¿Qué framework o qué adorno,
se oculta en mi container hoy?

[Coda]
Ya no existe la casa…
Ya no existen los viejos…
Solo el code está lejos…
Sufriendo el deploy pasa…

Docker…

— THE DOCTOR EMIS SONGBOOK (tango for coders, in Gardel's blood) —

videoTitle: Stop making temp files to compare two commands
videoDescription:
You wrote both outputs to /tmp, ran diff, and forgot to clean up. Your shell
has done this in one line for decades — it is called process substitution.

The shell runs each command and hands diff a filename that is really a pipe.
Nothing is written to disk, nothing to clean up.

The one that saves an afternoon — set difference without a script:

comm needs sorted input, so sort it inline.

The catch: it is not a real file. Check for yourself with ls -l (echo hi)
and you get /dev/fd/63 pointing at a pipe. Anything that needs to seek or
rewind the input will fail — and this is bash and zsh only, so your POSIX
sh script will not have it.

videoTitle: Your API isn't slow. One stage of it is. #shorts
videoDescription:
"time curl" gives you one number and zero suspects. curl -w breaks the same
request into DNS, TCP, TLS and server think time — so you stop blaming the
network and start blaming the right thing.

The catch: the numbers are cumulative from the start. Subtract to get each
stage. In this example 779ms of the 884ms total is the server thinking.

Two ways to fool yourself:
• No -o /dev/null and you're timing your terminal painting text
• The first call pays for DNS that every later call gets from cache
Run it three times before you believe any of it.

videoTitle: Find the commit that deleted your code
videoDescription:
A config line used to be there. It is gone, nobody remembers deleting it, and
git grep returns nothing — because grep only searches files as they are right
now. Deleted code is invisible to it.

git has a tool for exactly this. It is called the pickaxe:

  git log -S'DATABASE_URL' --oneline

-S finds the commits where the number of matches changed: the one that added
your line, and the one that took it away. Add -p to see the exact diff.

The distinction that trips people up:

  -S  fires when the match count changes
  -G  fires when the diff touches it at all

A line that merely moved keeps the count identical, so -S will not see it.
Reach for -G when you suspect a move rather than a deletion.

And the one almost nobody knows — replay every change a single function ever
saw, without guessing paths or diffing by hand:

  git log -L :handleAuth:app.py
